parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what power tells you about how quickly energy is being transferred - it is a rate with respect to which quantity?
parts.proper_answer: Power is the work done per unit time (rate of doing work).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Power Means**
Think of two identical cars climbing a hill, one fast and one slow. Both do the same work against gravity, but the faster one is more powerful. So power measures how fast work is done, not just how much.

Step 2: **Exact Definition**
In symbols, $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ where $W$ is work done and $t$ is time taken. So in words: power is work done per unit time, measured in watts ($\text{W}$) or $\text{J s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: The car moves at constant speed, so the forward driving force must exactly balance the 1750 N resistive force. Which power formula links a steady force and a steady velocity?
Hint 2: Check you are using $F = 1750\text{ N}$ and $v = 35\text{ m s}^{-1}$ together, then calculate and give power in $\text{W}$ to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force Needed for Constant Speed**
At constant velocity the resultant force is zero. That means the motor must push forward with a force equal in size to the total resistive force, so $F = 1750\text{ N}$ in the direction of motion.

Step 2: **Use P = Fv**
Power delivered by a force $F$ moving at velocity $v$ in the direction of $F$ is: $$P = Fv$$ Substitute the values: $$P = 1750 \times 35$$ $$P = 61250\text{ W} \approx 6.1 \times 10^4\text{ W}$$ This is the useful power transmitted to the wheels.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Useful work is done against the resistive force over the whole journey. What is the distance in SI base units (metres) rather than km?
Hint 2: Recall how work links force and distance moved in the direction of the force, then multiply by the converted distance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert Distance to Metres**
Work must be calculated in joules using metres. $$s = 17\text{ km} = 17 \times 1000 = 17000\text{ m}$$ A common slip is to use 17 directly.

Step 2: **Calculate Work Done**
Useful work done against a constant resistive force: $$W = Fs$$ $$W = 1750 \times 17000$$ $$W = 2.975 \times 10^7\text{ J} \approx 3.0 \times 10^7\text{ J}$$ Alternatively, $$W = Pt$$ with $t = s/v$ gives the same result.

parts.label: (b)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: P = V × I Power in = 600 × I
Efficiency = useful power output / (total) power input

hints: Hint 1: Start by separating the two powers: the useful mechanical power you found in (b)(i) is the output, while the electrical power supplied to the motor is the input. How is electrical power written using the 600 V p.d.?
Hint 2: Recall the efficiency relation that links useful output power and total input power for the 85% efficient motor.
Hint 3: Rearrange to make current $I$ the subject, remember to use 0.85 not 85, then substitute $6.1 \times 10^4\text{ W}$ and 600 V.
parts.proper_answer: Input power $P_{in} = VI = 600I$. Efficiency $= P_{out}/P_{in}$, so $0.85 = 6.1 \times 10^4/(600I)$, giving $I = 120\text{ A}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write Electrical Input Power**
The motor is driven electrically, so the total power supplied to it is: $$P_{in} = VI$$ where $V = 600\text{ V}$ and $I$ is the unknown current. So $$P_{in} = 600I$$

Step 2: **Apply Efficiency**
Efficiency is the fraction of input that becomes useful output: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$$ Here useful output is the $6.1 \times 10^4\text{ W}$ from (b)(i). So: $$0.85 = \frac{6.1 \times 10^4}{600 \times I}$$

Step 3: **Solve for Current**
Rearrange: $$I = \frac{6.1 \times 10^4}{0.85 \times 600}$$ $$I \approx 120\text{ A}$$ The current is larger than the ideal $P/V$ value because 15% of the input power is wasted, e.g. as heat.

parts.label: (c)(i)

markscheme_points.text: Air resistance is the same, as the speed is the same

hints: Hint 1: Air resistance (drag) depends mainly on speed and shape, not on whether the road is flat or sloped. Has either of those changed here?
parts.proper_answer: No change. Air resistance is the same because the speed is unchanged at $35\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Controls Air Resistance?**
For a given car shape, drag grows with speed through the air. The question states the car continues down the slope at the same speed as in (b), $35\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Since neither speed nor shape has changed, the air resistance stays the same. The slope itself does not directly alter drag.

parts.label: (c)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: The motor is producing less power (because of gravitational force / conversion of gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy) so the current will be smaller.

hints: Hint 1: Downhill, part of the weight now acts down the slope and helps drive the car forward, so think about whether the motor still needs to provide as much forward force and power at the same speed.
parts.proper_answer: Current decreases. Less motor power is needed because a component of weight acts down the slope (gravitational potential energy helps motion), so with $V$ constant and $P_{in}=VI$, $I$ is smaller.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the Motor Works Less Hard Downhill**
On the flat, the motor alone balances resistance. Down the slope, gravity provides a forward component of weight down the slope. So the motor needs to supply less forward force to keep the same constant speed, meaning less useful mechanical power $P = Fv$ is required from the motor.

Step 2: **Link to Current**
Since $V$ is still 600 V and input power is $P_{in} = VI$, a smaller required output power means a smaller input power and hence a smaller current $I$.

parts.question_text:
An electric car is powered by a motor. The car is travelling at a constant speed of 35 m s⁻¹ along a straight horizontal road, as shown in Fig. 3.1.
There is a total resistive force of 1750 N acting on the car.

parts.question_text:
Calculate the power transmitted to the wheels of the car by the motor.
